{"id": "2807054f-daa3-44c7-a0ad-27bb64c8211b", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_wFilj611syL6DVo1hnRwjc", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Configure a Direct Connect Classic connection\",\"context\":\"## (Recommended) Step 7: Configure redundant connections\\n\\nTo provide for failover, we recommend that you request and configure two dedicated\\nconnections to AWS, as shown in the following figure. These connections can terminate on\\none or two routers in your network.\\n\\nThere are different configuration choices available when you provision two\\ndedicated connections:\\n\\n* Active/Active (BGP multipath). This is the default configuration, where\\n both connections are active. Direct Connect supports multipathing to multiple\\n virtual interfaces within the same location, and traffic is load-shared\\n between interfaces based on flow. If one connection becomes unavailable, all\\n traffic is routed through the other connection.\\n* Active/Passive (failover). One connection is handling traffic, and the\\n other is on standby. If the active connection becomes unavailable, all traffic\\n is routed through the passive connection. You need to prepend the AS path to the\\n routes on one of your links for that to be the passive link.\\n\\nHow you configure the connections doesn't affect redundancy, but it does affect\\nthe policies that determine how your data is routed over both connections. We recommend\\nthat you configure both connections as active.\\n\\nIf you use a VPN connection for redundancy, ensure that you implement a health check\\nand failover mechanism. If you use either of the following configurations, then you need\\nto check your route table routing to route to the new network interface.\\n\\n* You use your own instances for routing, for example the instance is the\\n firewall.\\n* You use your own instance that terminates a VPN connection.\\n\\nTo achieve high availability, we strongly recommend that you configure connections to\\ndifferent Direct Connect locations.\\n\\nFor more information about Direct Connect resiliency, see Direct Connect Resiliency Recommendations\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/toolkit-classic.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"How do I set an Active/Passive Direct Connect connection to AWS?\",\"context\":\"Resolution\\n-----------\\n\\nWhen using Direct Connect to transport production workloads to and from AWS, it's a best practice to use dual Direct Connect connections using different data centers or providers.\\n\\nConfigure the following:\\n\\n* Two routers to terminate the primary and secondary Direct Connect\u00a0connections to avoid a single point of device failure.\\n* A private virtual interface on each of the Direct Connect\u00a0routers that terminate to the same Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC).\\n* High availability routing protocols (such as HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP) on two routers to allow local servers to use multiple routers that act as a single virtual router. This configuration helps you to maintain connectivity even if the primary router fails. \\n-or- \\nRun an internal routing protocol (such as Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) that learns routes from Direct Connect external BGP gateways and distributes prefixes to internal BGP gateways.\\n* Active/Passive (failover). In this scenario, one connection handles traffic, and the other is on standby. If the active connection becomes unavailable, all traffic is routed through the passive connection. You must use Autonomous System (AS) prepending for the routes on one of your links to set it as the passive link.\\n\\nFor more information, see [Configure redundant connections](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/dev-test-resiliency.html).\\n\\n**Note:** Check your vendor documentation for commands that are specific to your network device\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/active-passive-direct-connect\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"How do I set up an Active/Passive Direct Connect connection to AWS?\",\"context\":\"Resolution\\n----------\\n\\n**Note:** It's a best practice to use dual Direct Connect connections through different data centers or providers to transport production workloads to and from AWS.\\n\\nConfigure the following:\\n\\n* Two routers on an on-premises location to terminate the primary and secondary Direct Connect connections to avoid a single point of device failure.\\n* A private VIF on each of the Direct Connect routers that terminate to the same Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC).\\n* High availability routing protocols (such as HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP) on two routers. This allows local servers to use multiple routers that act as a single virtual router. This configuration helps maintain connectivity even if the primary router fails. You can also run an internal routing protocol such as Border Gateway Protocol (BGP).\\n* In an Active/Passive Direct Connect setup (failover), an active connection handles traffic and a passive connection is on standby. If the active connection becomes unavailable, then all traffic must be routed through the passive connection. Use Autonomous System (AS) prepending for the routes on one of your links to set the link as passive.\\n\\n**Note:** Check your vendor documentation for commands that are specific to your network device.\\n\\nFor more information on configuring redundant Direct Connect connections on AWS, see [Configure redundant connections](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/getting_started.html#RedundantConnections)\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/direct-connect-active-passive-connection\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verify AWS docs on Direct Connect BGP failover direction requirements"}

{"id": "0c45c401-dda5-40a1-8e4d-3919047d6ec6", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Both directions matter, but for different reasons — you need to check each one independently because failover in one direction doesn't guarantee failover in the other:

**Outbound (AWS → on-premises) — routes you advertise to AWS**
- Controlled via AS path prepending on the routes you send to AWS over BGP.
- If you want a VIF to be passive/backup, you prepend your AS number on that path so AWS's BGP path selection prefers the shorter path via the primary VIF.
- Audit check: confirm the backup VIF actually has prepending configured — if both VIFs advertise routes with equal AS path length, you get active/active (ECMP) instead of the intended active/passive behavior, which may not be what the design assumes.

**Inbound (on-premises ← AWS) — routes AWS advertises to you**
- AWS advertises VPC/prefix routes to your router over BGP on each VIF independently.
- Your on-premises router's local preference/weight or AS path prepending on your side determines which VIF it prefers for return traffic.
- Audit check: confirm your router is actually configured to deprioritize the backup VIF's inbound routes the same way — otherwise you can end up with asymmetric routing, where outbound traffic fails over correctly but inbound traffic still tries to use the dead link (or vice versa).

**Why check both independently**
BGP path selection is per-direction and per-device — AWS's decision about which path to send traffic down, and your router's decision about which path to send traffic down, are two separate policy evaluations. A common misconfiguration is prepending correctly on one side (say, your outbound advertisement to AWS) but forgetting the mirrored config on the other, which produces asymmetric failover: traffic drains one direction but not the other when the primary VIF goes down, leaving the connection effectively half-broken during a failure.

If you're auditing actual VIFs in your account, I can pull the BGP configurations and advertised routes for your Direct Connect connections to check this — want me to do that?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
